connections.why: The same comparison now follows complete simulated shifts rather than individual static predictions.

reflection.prompt: Which randomness can genuinely be shared when actions change the future?
reflection.carryForward: State the coupling and reserve fresh scenarios for assessment.

simulation-system-identification.premise: The simulator’s structure is plausible, but its gain does not match the measured conveyor.

construction.title: Estimate the unknown parameter
construction.start: Keep command-response agreement and command energy on separate dot-product branches.
construction.outcome: The fitted value is tied to measured excitation rather than a guessed constant.
hints: The fitted gain should explain all command-response pairs together under the stated through-origin model. It is not the average response or the average of separate response-to-command ratios.
Use the dot product of commands with responses on one branch and commands with themselves on the other. Their ratio fits the shared gain when the commands contain nonzero excitation.

investigation.title: One response changes from four to five
investigation.question: Predict the fitted gain for commands [1,2] and responses [2,5].
investigation.outcome: The fit becomes 2.4; it does not match both observations exactly.

connections.why: We now learn a parameter inside a declared system model.

connections.skill: Fit a relationship from paired measurements
connections.why: The fit is restricted to a physically motivated through-origin form.

reflection.prompt: What residual pattern would suggest a delay instead of a wrong gain?
reflection.carryForward: Use failed predictions to question model structure as well as parameter values.

simulation-transfer-checks.premise: A policy trained on default conditions fails when friction changes.

construction.title: Keep the difficult condition visible
construction.start: Calculate the mean tested cost and the largest tested cost on separate branches. Return them in that order so the individual-condition requirement can be considered beside the average.
construction.outcome: Average improvement cannot erase the worst observed condition.
hints: An ordinary average can hide a difficult condition. Keep the mean and the worst tested cost visible separately.
Build a mean branch and a maximum branch from the same cost list, returning them in that order. A maximum over these tested conditions cannot establish safety in every untested environment.

investigation.title: One condition becomes much harder
investigation.question: Does a mean below eight allow us to ignore the cost of twelve?
investigation.outcome: Preserve the failure for development, then test the repaired policy on a new condition.

options.label: No; inspect the independent condition requirement
options.feedback: The low-friction case fails even if an aggregate seems acceptable.

options.label: Yes; the mean is the whole deployment
options.feedback: The deployment weighting and hard requirements must be justified separately.

connections.why: The learned system parameter may change when the operating condition changes.
Repeated scenario evidence helps separate a condition failure from sampling variation.

reflection.prompt: Which real-world mechanism is missing from the simulator entirely?
reflection.carryForward: Validate the simulator and reserve fresh conditions before claiming transfer.

numerical-stable-normalisation.premise: A new encoder changes numerical scale and breaks the normalisation Botie used for retrieval.

construction.title: Protect the products before they are formed
construction.start: Reuse the vector-length calculation, but move a common rescaling in front of its squares.
construction.outcome: The direction stays the same across a large change in magnitude.
hints: Start with the largest absolute component. It gives a common scale, rather than a separate scale for every coordinate.
A zero vector needs a deliberate policy. Use the nonzero-divisor tool at the scale and scaled-length divisions so zeros remain zeros.

investigation.title: The first length calculation becomes infinite
investigation.question: Which part of the earlier construction lost the direction?
investigation.outcome: Repair the calculation before interpreting the retrieval result.

options.label: The squares overflowed before the final division
options.feedback: The original components were finite. Changing their scale before multiplying avoids that intermediate failure.

options.label: Every large embedding must have zero relevance
options.feedback: Numerical failure is not evidence about whether a document answers the question.

connections.why: We preserve that same geometric comparison while changing its numerical evaluation.

reflection.prompt: What other failure could remain even after every output direction has length one?
reflection.carryForward: Keep encoder compatibility and retrieval relevance as separate checks from numerical range.

numerical-identifiable-models.premise: The fitted simulator uses two heater gains that the original combined measurements never identified.

construction.title: Construct a test of the competing fits
construction.start: Reuse matrix-times-vector twice, retaining one prediction per candidate experiment. Keep positions only after comparing the aligned gaps.
construction.outcome: The suggested experiments are tied to a specific unresolved parameter difference.
hints: Both branches must use the same candidate experiment rows and the same coordinate order.
Subtract the two prediction vectors before taking absolute values. Compare those gaps with the planning resolution, then retain passing original positions.

investigation.title: The next batch runs the heaters together again
investigation.question: Did the larger record count resolve which heater contributes more?
investigation.outcome: Change the proposed experiment, not just the file size.

options.label: No; both candidates still predict the same totals
options.feedback: These new rows repeat the same combination of inputs. More records need not add an independent direction.

options.label: Yes; every extra row identifies another parameter
options.feedback: Repeated dependent rows can leave the same ambiguity.

connections.why: A returned parameter estimate now needs a check that the experiments could determine it.

connections.skill: Apply one coefficient vector to many rows
connections.why: The same matrix calculation compares candidate predictions at proposed experiments.

reflection.prompt: If a new measurement rejects both candidates, what assumptions would you inspect?
reflection.carryForward: Preserve model alternatives and measurement resolution when planning new evidence.

numerical-gradient-checks.premise: Botie’s symmetric gradient check conceals an absolute-loss corner behind a zero.

construction.title: Keep the two local comparisons separate
construction.start: Reuse the loss evaluation and subtraction tools to measure each side before averaging.
construction.outcome: The report explains why a central zero can have different meanings.
hints: Build weight-minus-step and weight-plus-step before evaluating the loss. Each loss machine uses the same target and kind.
The left slope uses centre-minus-left; the right uses right-minus-centre. Their average is the central difference, which must not replace the separate evidence.

investigation.title: The loss changes to absolute error at its target
investigation.question: Does the central zero establish a classical derivative of zero?
investigation.outcome: Retain both sides before judging the implementation’s derivative convention.

options.label: No; inspect the opposite one-sided slopes
options.feedback: The two sides approach different slopes at this corner.

options.label: Yes; a central estimate always proves differentiability
options.feedback: Symmetric cancellation can hide a nondifferentiable point.

connections.why: We now approximate that local relationship from evaluations of the running program.
An independent finite-difference fixture helps diagnose a reported derivative without replacing training.

reflection.prompt: Which changes to randomness or state would make these perturbations compare different losses?
reflection.carryForward: Keep the loss definition, numerical scale and derivative convention attached to a gradient-check result.

numerical-adaptive-steps.premise: The simulator’s old fixed timestep misses a rapid change that its learned training target must represent.

construction.title: Build an acceptance test around the old update
construction.start: Reuse the Euler update, then add a midpoint reevaluation and an explicit error comparison before the result is accepted.
construction.outcome: A failed attempt has a visible numerical reason rather than silently entering the training trajectory.
hints: The fine branch must take its second half step from the midpoint output, not from the original state again.
Compute the error magnitude and tolerance on separate branches. For Threshold gate, supply tolerance first and error second so acceptance means the allowance is at least the estimate.

investigation.title: The proposed interval grows from a tenth of a second to one second
investigation.question: Will the discrepancy remain inside the same absolute-plus-relative tolerance?
investigation.outcome: The larger interval is rejected. Retry it from the unchanged starting state.

connections.why: The same update becomes a component inside a check of its local approximation.

connections.skill: Keep the procedure that produced training records
connections.why: Solver method and tolerance belong beside the simulator version and generated data.

reflection.prompt: What separate evidence would tell us whether the physical cooling law is wrong?
reflection.carryForward: Track local numerical acceptance separately from complete-trajectory error and agreement with measured equipment.
